week.t: NASA: the Roman Space Telescope’s instruments are aligned; next, more than 3,000 moving parts in its coronagraph’s deformable mirrors
NASA station blog: Menon and Watkins pack Dragon for a Pacific splashdown; still no departure date
ESA’s Euclid releases 1.7 million GB of data: over 900 million galaxies and 15,000 strong-lens candidates
PIB: a new deep-sea shark, Echinorhinus roinee, named from trawler bycatch landed at Kollam, Kerala
A*STAR Research: 3D-printed steel beams warp up or down depending on a 1.3 mm thickness threshold
CERN: construction begins on DUNE’s first cryostat, 17,000 tonnes of liquid argon 1.5 km under South Dakota

tiles.cap: 900 million galaxies in one release: Euclid maps sky the size of 9,500 full Moons
tiles.nums: of data in Euclid’s first big release, from about 13 months of observing: more than a billion objects, over 900 million of them galaxies
tiles.p1: On Thursday 12 November the European Space Agency released the first major batch of data from Euclid, its €1.4 billion space telescope: 1.7 million GB from about 13 months of observing, covering 1,900 square degrees of sky, the area of 9,500 full Moons and about 14% of the planned survey. In it are more than a billion objects, over 900 million galaxies, some 15,000 candidate strong gravitational lenses and over 60 million candidate quasars. Euclid’s images are about four times sharper than today’s ground telescopes manage.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: those 15,000 lens candidates are the largest catalogue of strong cosmic lenses ever assembled, Physics World reports; the first full data release is due in mid-2027.
deep: Where it sits

Euclid launched in July 2023 and observes from Lagrange point L2, about 1.5 million km from Earth, with a 1.2 m telescope feeding a camera and a spectrometer. Routine surveying began in February 2024; a preliminary release in 2025 covered about 60 square degrees.
Who

The Euclid Consortium has about 2,600 members from more than 15 countries. “This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind,” said Carole Mundell, ESA’s Director of Science. Valeria Pettorino, the project scientist: “This unlocks ground-breaking science.”
Try the scale

If 1,900 square degrees is about 14% of the planned survey, divide 1,900 by 0.14 and you have the size of the whole survey in square degrees. One full Moon covers about a fifth of a square degree, which is where the 9,500 comes from: 1,900 ÷ 9,500.
The picture

Abell 3128, a cluster of hundreds of galaxies around 800 million light-years away, as Euclid sees it. Image: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, processed by J.-C. Cuillandre and E. Bertin, CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO.
tiles.src: Physics World, 12 Nov 2026 (Michael Banks): ESA’s Euclid mission unveils treasure trove of cosmic data
tiles.credit: Photo: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA; J.-C. Cuillandre, E. Bertin (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

tiles.cap: Roman is aligned to a fraction of a hair’s breadth. Next: 3,000 moving parts in one mirror
tiles.nums: in Roman’s Wide Field Instrument, each remapped after launch so they lock onto guide stars together
tiles.p1: NASA said on Friday 13 November that the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, launched in August, has finished aligning its instruments. Launch vibrations, temperature changes and the move into weightlessness shift things slightly, so test observations were used to update the telescope’s internal map; the team also adjusted the secondary mirror and a smaller mirror to sharpen the Coronagraph Instrument’s view. “Roman is now internally aligned to within a tiny fraction of a hair’s breadth of perfection,” said Tony Sohn of the Space Telescope Science Institute.
tiles.p2: Why it is hard: Roman has to be “at least ten times more stable” than Hubble or Webb, says Dominic Benford, the programme scientist, because the coronagraph has to stare at one star for a long time.
deep: Why things move

Rockets shake, space is cold and gravity is gone, so the detectors sit only roughly where they were set on the ground. The 18 detectors “are meant to work together when we’re locking onto guide stars,” said Tyler Desjardins of the Space Telescope Science Institute, so each one’s position had to be mapped again.
3,000 moving parts

Next the team works through more than 3,000 tiny moving parts in the coronagraph’s deformable mirrors, then begins the second stage of active starlight control: cancelling a star’s glare so something faint beside it can show. “The wave nature of light makes starlight spill when forming images,” said Brian Kern, an optical engineer at JPL. “We have demonstrated this in a lab using an artificial space environment.”
Two at once
While the coronagraph observes, the Wide Field Instrument guides, and that guiding time yields extra deep-field images. No date for the start of science has been given yet.
The picture
NASA’s alignment animation from the Roman Fine Guidance Sensor team: stars that began off-centre in Roman’s guide windows slide into line as small adjustments are made.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Roman blog, 13 Nov 2026: Instruments on NASA’s Roman Space Telescope Get in Sync for Science · JPL, 30 Aug 2026: NASA’s Dark Universe-Seeking Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launches
tiles.credit: Image: NASA / Roman Space Telescope Fine Guidance Sensor team

tiles.cap: Coming down in Dragon: 3D-printed blood vessels, bacterial DNA, lamps that fake daylight
tiles.nums: of science, supplies and hardware Dragon delivered to the station on 15 October; NASA’s blog still gives no date for its return, only that it is nearing the end of its stay
tiles.p1: NASA’s station blog for Thursday 12 November says the SpaceX Dragon cargo craft is nearing the end of its stay; the crew is loading it for a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, with the last items packed the day before departure. Going down: experiment samples including bacterial DNA and 3D-printed blood vessels, and a set of lighting hardware built to recreate natural daylight and regulate the crew’s sleep, returning after more than three years of testing. Anil Menon and Jessica Watkins began loading payloads; Menon and Joshua Kutryk rearranged cargo to balance its mass and centre of gravity for re-entry.
tiles.p2: Why it is interesting: the last things in are research samples in portable freezers and incubators, loaded shortly before departure.
deep: Friday’s work

On Friday 13 November Luke Delaney harvested thale cress plants grown in the Multi-use Variable-g Platform in Japan’s Kibo module and preserved samples in the Life Science Glovebox for return to Earth; Menon and Watkins kept packing Dragon; Watkins activated student-designed hardware that tests physical, chemical and biological processes in microgravity.
Spacesuit laundry
Delaney cleaned the cooling and ventilation systems in two spacesuits worn on the 29 October and 5 November spacewalks, which installed roll-out solar arrays on the station.
What NASA has not said

No undocking or splashdown date and no mission number appear on the blog; the 13 October launch release said Dragon would stay until mid-November and splash down off the coast of California. The crew of seven: station commander Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov of Roscosmos, Menon, Watkins and Delaney of NASA, and Kutryk of the Canadian Space Agency.
The photo
Anil Menon during the 29 October spacewalk, helmet lights on, installing a roll-out solar array on the station’s port truss; photographed by Luke Delaney.
tiles.src: NASA space station blog, 12 Nov 2026: Crew Packs Dragon with Science and Cleans Spacesuits · 13 Nov 2026: Botany, Biomedicine, and Cargo Ops Wrap Up Week Aboard Station

tiles.cap: Voyager 1 is one light-day away next week. NASA wants your phone to flash it on Tuesday
tiles.nums: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km) from Earth: from Wednesday, light, and any radio command, will take 24 hours to reach Voyager 1
tiles.p1: On Wednesday 18 November, NASA says, Voyager 1 will have travelled one light-day from Earth: more than 16 billion miles (25.9 billion km), so far that light from Earth takes 24 hours to reach it. The evening before, Tuesday 17 November, NASA is asking people everywhere to make a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet after sunset, “Shine Bright for Voyager’s Light-Day”. A NASA web page makes a phone or tablet flash VGR, Voyager’s call sign, in Morse code.
tiles.p2: Why now: NASA announced the activities on Tuesday 10 November. A panel from JPL is streamed on NASA’s site on Friday 20 November at 1 am Singapore time (Thursday noon US Eastern).
deep: Who is talking

The discussion at JPL’s von Kármán Auditorium in Southern California includes Nicky Fox, NASA’s associate administrator for science; Jonathan Lunine, JPL’s chief scientist; Suzanne Dodd, the Voyager project manager; Linda Spilker, the Voyager project scientist; Kareem Badaruddin, the Voyager mission manager; and Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, the deputy project scientist. It takes questions and is streamed live.
A film is coming
NASA says the event previews a Voyager documentary on NASA+ planned for 2027, the mission’s 50th anniversary.
Which day, exactly

NASA’s Voyager page gives the moment: 5:16:07 am US Eastern on Wednesday 18 November, which is 6:16 pm in Singapore, at 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 km) from Earth. Its November skywatching chart puts Voyager 1 in the constellation Ophiuchus, toward the western horizon at about 5 pm on the 17th: you cannot see the probe, but you can face it.
Where the picture comes from
The image is an artist’s concept of a Voyager spacecraft from NASA/JPL-Caltech; no camera is out there to photograph it.
tiles.src: NASA release M26-086, 10 Nov 2026 (Gerelle Q. Dodson): NASA Invites Media, Public to Join Voyager 1 One-Light Day Activities · NASA Science: Voyager 1: What Is a Light-Day · What’s Up: November 2026

tiles.cap: Leonids before dawn Tuesday and Wednesday, up to 15 an hour. Mars meets Jupiter at dawn
tiles.nums: Leonid meteors under ideal skies in the early hours of 17 and 18 November, after the Moon has set; most people will see fewer
tiles.p1: NASA’s skywatching notes for November put the Leonid meteor shower at its best in the early morning hours of Tuesday 17 and Wednesday 18 November, after the Moon sets: up to about 15 meteors an hour under ideal conditions, fewer for most viewers. Around 12 November the Northern Taurids peaked at a gentler 5 an hour. And on the mornings of 15 and 16 November Mars and Jupiter stand about 1.2° apart in the south-east before sunrise, Jupiter the brighter, Mars reddish beside it.
tiles.p2: Why now: New Moon was 8 November and first quarter is 17 November; NASA says to look after the Moon sets.
deep: Watch several mornings
NASA suggests watching Mars and Jupiter on more than one morning, to see them close in and then separate again. Jupiter is the brighter of the two.
Three supermoons
The full Moon of 24 November is a supermoon, the first of three in a row: November, December and January. Third quarter follows on 30 November.
Faced the right way
NASA’s chart for 17 November also marks where Voyager 1 sits, in Ophiuchus toward the western horizon at about 5 pm, the evening before it reaches one light-day from Earth.
The photo
NASA’s page opens with the full Moon rising over Vasquez Rocks, north of Los Angeles, photographed by Preston Dyches of NASA on 24 June 2021.
tiles.src: NASA Science, What’s Up: November 2026 Skywatching Tips from NASA (Raquel Villanueva, JPL), 2 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: San Diego’s sea 2.80 ft above its normal high mark on 27 Oct, a record. Next: 22–27 Nov
tiles.nums: above Mean Higher High Water at NOAA’s San Diego tide gauge on 27 October 2026, the highest level ever observed there
tiles.p1: Between 24 and 30 October, NOAA tide gauges at four California stations recorded their highest water levels ever observed: San Diego 2.80 ft above Mean Higher High Water on 27 October, Los Angeles 2.70 ft, La Jolla 2.65 ft and Santa Barbara 2.65 ft. Santa Monica’s 2.72 ft was its second highest, Port San Luis’s 2.35 ft its fourth, Monterey’s 2.20 ft its seventh. Three things stacked up: a perigean spring tide, with the full Moon at its closest to Earth; El Niño Kelvin waves that raise sea level along the coast by 6 to 12 inches or more for weeks; and a marine heatwave, because “warmer water takes up more space than cold water.”
tiles.p2: Why now: NOAA predicts the next above-normal tides for 22–27 November and 22–26 December 2026; the full Moon of 24 November is a supermoon.
deep: Three causes, one week

A perigean spring tide happens when a full or new Moon coincides with the Moon’s closest approach to Earth; El Niño sends Kelvin waves across the Pacific that lift sea level at the coast for weeks; and a marine heatwave expands the water itself. NOAA says the high water inundated the state’s low-lying areas.
What the gauges measure

Mean Higher High Water is the gauge’s reference level for a normal high tide, so 2.80 ft above it is water far past where a high tide usually stops. The seven stations named are all on NOAA’s network along the California coast.
The photo
A microwave water-level sensor at NOAA’s La Jolla, California tide gauge, one of the stations that set a record.
tiles.src: NOAA National Ocean Service, 4 Nov 2026: California water levels break records · NASA What’s Up: November 2026 (supermoon)

tiles.cap: A 3-metre shark from 400 m down off Kerala turns out to be a species nobody had named
tiles.nums: depth on the continental slope where the Indian Bramble Shark lives; it grows up to three metres long
tiles.p1: Indian scientists have named a new deep-sea shark, Echinorhinus roinee, the Indian Bramble Shark, the government’s Press Information Bureau announced on Wednesday 11 November. It lives on the continental slope at 350 to 450 m, grows up to three metres, is dark brown to blackish, and its skin carries thorn-like denticles that fuse into multi-pointed plates as it ages. For years it had been taken for the Atlantic bramble shark, Echinorhinus brucus; measurements and mitochondrial DNA barcoding show a distinct Indian Ocean lineage.
tiles.p2: Where it came from: specimens landed as bycatch by deep-sea shrimp trawlers at Sakthikulangara fishing harbour in Kollam district, Kerala.
deep: Who

Researchers at the Zoological Survey of India and ICAR’s Central Marine Fisheries Research Institute, funded by the Ministry of Earth Sciences under the Deep Ocean Mission. The description is published in Records of the Zoological Survey of India; the type specimens are kept at ZSI’s Marine Biology Regional Centre in Chennai.
How you tell

Compared with its relatives it has larger eyes, larger pelvic fins and a longer stretch from snout to gills. Its DNA separates it from E. brucus in the Atlantic and E. cookei, the prickly shark of the Pacific; similar genetic records suggest its range may extend to Oman, Sri Lanka and Thailand.
The name

“The Indian Bramble Shark is a distinct species,” said Dr Dhriti Banerjee, Director of ZSI; of the old identification, “our measurements and DNA evidence show otherwise.” The species name roinee honours her daughter, Roinee.
tiles.src: Press Information Bureau, Government of India, 11 Nov 2026: Indian Scientists Discover New Deep-Sea Shark Species in the Indian Ocean (ZSI and ICAR-CMFRI)
tiles.credit: Photo: Press Information Bureau / Zoological Survey of India

tiles.cap: Warm a metre of copper by 100 °C: it grows 1.7 mm. That is why hot water loosens jar lids
tiles.nums: the fraction of its length a copper rod gains for every 1 °C it warms, the Exploratorium says: 1.7 mm per metre over a 100 °C change
tiles.p1: Atoms in a warm solid vibrate more and sit slightly farther apart, so the whole thing grows. The Exploratorium’s Cool Hot Rod makes the growth visible: very hot tap water is poured through a copper tube whose far end rests on a needle, and as the tube lengthens it rolls the needle, which turns a toothpick stuck through its eye like a pointer. Copper expands by 1.7 × 10⁻⁵ of its length per degree Celsius, so over a 100 °C change a 1 m tube gains about 1.7 mm, enough to turn an average needle more than two full revolutions. Pour cold water through and the pointer turns back.
tiles.p2: Test it at home: a stuck metal jar lid loosens under hot water because the lid expands more than the glass; cold water on hot glass can crack it because the glass expands unevenly.
deep: The recipe

1 to 2 m of 6 mm copper tubing with a funnel joined to one end by a short plastic tube. Clamp the funnel end to a block on the table; rest the other end on a second block with a needle between tube and block, at right angles to the tube; push a toothpick through the needle’s eye; put a bucket under the end. Pour very hot tap water in and watch which way the toothpick tilts, then pour cold.
Why a needle
The tube moves only about 1.7 mm, but a needle is thin, so that much rolling is more than two full turns, and the toothpick amplifies the motion so you can see it.
Where it is used
Thermometers and thermostats work on expansion, the Exploratorium notes; so do the stuck jar lid and the cracked glass.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks: Cool Hot Rod

tiles.cap: 17,000 t of argon at −185 °C, 1.5 km down, waiting for neutrinos fired from 1,300 km away
tiles.nums: from Fermilab in Batavia, Illinois, to the DUNE far detectors at the Sanford Underground Research Facility in Lead, South Dakota
tiles.p1: Nearly 1.5 km underground in South Dakota, crews from Fermilab, CERN and the Sanford Underground Research Facility have begun building the first of two giant cryostats for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment, CERN reported on Tuesday 10 November. Each is an insulated container 66 m long, 19 m wide and 18 m high that will hold about 17,000 tonnes of liquid argon at about −185 °C. Its frame uses 2,600 red steel beams, part of more than 6,200 tonnes of steel contributed by CERN and carried one by one from the surface down to the assembly area. From 2031 a neutrino beam from Fermilab, 1,300 km away, is expected to reach it.
tiles.p2: Why: neutrinos may explain why the Universe ended up mostly matter; the detector will also watch particles arriving from the Sun and from deep space.
deep: Timeline

Assembly of the second cryostat starts in 2027 in the North Cavern; the underground spaces are completed in 2029, the detector in 2030, and the beam arrives in 2031. The experiment is slated to run until the late 2040s. More than 1,500 researchers are in the collaboration today, 1,800 from 2030.
Who said what

“DUNE is Fermilab’s top priority,” said Norbert Holtkamp, the director of Fermilab. “SURF is proud to support this world-class research 1478 metres below ground level,” said Mike Headley, the lab’s director. “This brings us one step closer to science,” said Jolie Macier, project manager for the far detectors and cryogenics.
CERN’s part

“Collaboration is in CERN’s DNA, and our contribution to DUNE is a brilliant example of cross-organisational partnership,” said Mark Thomson, CERN’s Director-General. The steel came from CERN as an in-kind contribution; Lluís Miralles, principal project engineer of CERN’s Neutrino Platform, is quoted on the build.
The picture
Construction of the first cryostat began in early November, photographed by Matthew Kapust of SURF.
tiles.src: CERN, 10 Nov 2026: Construction begins on massive underground neutrino experiment designed to unlock the secrets of the Universe
tiles.credit: Photo: Matthew Kapust, SURF, via CERN

tiles.cap: A $59 concrete-grey puck with no battery. Tap your phone on it, or your apps stay locked
tiles.nums: Brick has no battery, no charger and no Wi-Fi: an NFC chip in a magnetic puck is the physical key that unlocks the apps you have blocked
tiles.p1: TIME’s Best Inventions 2026 list includes Brick, built by TJ Driver, then 23, and his college friend Zach Nasgowitz: an app that blocks whatever apps you choose, and a small concrete-coloured puck with an NFC chip inside. To unlock the blocked apps you have to walk to the puck and physically tap your phone on it. Driver’s reason: his phone “was getting in the way.” The puck needs no battery, no charging and no Wi-Fi; it has a magnet and an anti-slip silicone base, and one puck works with any number of phones. Android 12 or iOS 17 and up; $59.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: Tom’s Guide’s Ashley Thieme says it “relies on human traits of laziness”, that with five emergency unbricks on hand, being able to turn blocks off in the app “doesn’t create that much of a barrier”, and that it is not going to “win any design awards”. Also: “If you don’t have the willpower to wait it out, this may not be for you.”
deep: The engineering

Tom’s Guide notes the chip is NFC, not RFID, so the phone has to be held close; the puck measures 2 × 2 inches and weighs 3.17 ounces. TIME’s line: often the tap is “all the friction needed to get you to do something other than doomscroll.”
Modes and escape hatches
Up to 10 custom modes; a remote lock by holding the virtual Brick in the app for 5 seconds; five Emergency Unbricks included, each of which unblocks everything without the puck. No recurring fees.
The numbers do not all agree

Brick’s product page says iOS 17.0 or later; its FAQ says iOS 18.0 or later. The company quotes a survey of more than 3,500 users in which over 95% felt less distracted; that is the maker’s own survey.
Praise
Tom’s Guide gave it an Editor’s Choice badge: “The Brick offers the best way to curb excessive phone usage,” and “effective at reducing screen time and social media usage.” A rival, Bloom, costs $39.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Daniel Varghese): Brick · getbrick.com product page and FAQ · Tom’s Guide review (Ashley Thieme, 2 Oct 2026)

tiles.cap: Nikon’s ZR: 540 g, 6K video, RED colour science, $2,199.95. Reviewers’ catch: the screen
tiles.nums: audio: Nikon calls the ZR the world’s first interchangeable-lens camera to record 32-bit float sound through both built-in and external microphones, promising distortion-free sound from quiet to loud
tiles.p1: TIME put the Nikon ZR (it calls it the Nikon Red ZR) on its Best Inventions 2026 list: a full-frame cinema camera, about 540 g body-only and 630 g with battery and card, 133 × 80.5 × 48.7 mm, co-developed with RED Digital Cinema, the high-end camera maker that is a Nikon subsidiary. Inside is a 24.5-megapixel full-frame sensor (35.9 × 23.9 mm) recording 6K at up to 60 frames a second and 4K at up to 120, in a new RAW format called R3D NE that carries RED’s colour science with no external recorder. The 4-inch screen is rated at 1,000 nits; price from $2,199.95.
tiles.p2: What reviewers found wrong: TechRadar’s Timothy Coleman says the screen is flip-out only, there is no viewfinder, no grip or mounting points for accessories, and the HDMI port is micro, not full-size. He ran into no overheating, though there are no vents or fans.
deep: Two base ISOs
The sensor has two native sensitivities, ISO 800 and ISO 6400, selectable in R3D NE recording; Nikon rates the dynamic range at 15+ stops.
32-bit float

Ordinary audio clips when a sound is too loud. 32-bit float records such a wide range that the level can be set afterwards; Nikon calls the ZR the world’s first interchangeable-lens camera to do this through both built-in and external microphones. The built-in mics offer five pickup patterns, including binaural.
The numbers do not all agree

Nikon’s US page lists the body at 1.18 lb (535 g) in one table and 1.19 lb in another, where Nikon’s launch release says about 540 g, and a maximum recording time of 360 minutes for some non-RAW settings but 125 minutes in its Tech Specs table. TechRadar calls the sensor “partially stacked”; Nikon’s own pages do not use that phrase.
Praise

TechRadar: “no other cinema camera comes close to the ZR for video features” at its price, with scores of Price 5/5, Design 4/5, Performance 4.5/5 and Image and video quality 4.5/5. Cards: CFexpress Type B plus microSD. TIME’s pitch: “an ultra-lightweight, full-frame camera designed for emerging cinematographers and high-end content producers.”
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026: Nikon Red ZR · Nikon ZR spec page (nikonusa.com) · Nikon news release, 10 Sep 2025 · TechRadar review (Timothy Coleman, updated 18 Dec 2025)

tiles.cap: Printed steel warps up above 1.3 mm thick, down below it. A*STAR saw what simulations miss
tiles.nums: the thickness at which the warp flips: stainless-steel beams printed parallel to the recoater blade bent upward when thicker, downward when thinner
tiles.p1: Metal 3D printing by laser powder bed fusion builds a part layer by layer: a blade called the recoater spreads a thin layer of metal powder, a laser melts the shape, and the blade sweeps again. A*STAR researchers found that stainless-steel beams printed parallel to the blade’s sweep warped upward when thicker than about 1.3 mm and downward when thinner, while beams rotated 90 degrees were much less sensitive to thickness. The cause, they say, is the repeated mechanical disturbance of the blade passing over the growing part, layer after layer.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: a common simulation predicted almost identical bending for both orientations, 1.69 mm and 1.67 mm, and so missed the difference entirely.
deep: How they measured

X-ray diffraction read the stress at the surface, and contour mapping reconstructed the stress locked inside the beams. “We wanted to show direct evidence linking residual stress to deformation,” said Pan Wang, Senior Scientist at A*STAR’s Singapore Institute of Manufacturing Technology.
The blade

“The repeated coating introduces additional mechanical disturbance and shear effects layer after layer,” said Chen Wang, also a Senior Scientist at SIMTech. Machine-learning models trained on 64 experimental data points now predict the deflection; next they will test laser power and layer thickness.
Who
A*STAR SIMTech with Osaka University, Xi’an Jiaotong University and NTU, published in Additive Manufacturing (volume 121, 2026) and reported by A*STAR Research on Wednesday 11 November.
tiles.src: A*STAR Research, 11 Nov 2026: When metal prints bend the rules · Additive Manufacturing 121, 105158 (2026)

tiles.cap: NTU glue cured from inside by magnetic nanoparticles. One hour matched 24 hours in an oven
tiles.nums: adhesive coatings cured by magnetic induction for one hour reached bonding strength comparable to coatings baked in a conventional oven for 24 hours, NTU reports
tiles.p1: Paints, glues and resins on car and aircraft parts are usually cured by putting the whole component into an industrial oven. NTU’s alternative, called Spinheat, mixes specially designed magnetic nanoparticles into the coating; an alternating magnetic field makes the particles generate heat inside the material, so the coating cures from within and heat-sensitive parts are spared. On Thursday 12 November NTU announced a partnership with Motherson, a design, engineering and manufacturing company with more than 475 facilities in 47 countries, to take it towards the factory floor.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: in the lab, one hour under the magnetic field matched 24 hours in an oven, and NTU says it could cut energy use, carbon emissions and the space taken up by curing equipment.
deep: Who and how

Professor Raju V. Ramanujan and Associate Professor Terry Steele of NTU’s School of Materials Science and Engineering lead the work; NTU first demonstrated magnetic-field-activated epoxy curing in 2020. The latest version reads the temperature in real time and adjusts the field, delivering heat only when needed, to reduce overheating, bubbles and other defects.
Next

“The next challenge is to understand how this can work reliably within automotive manufacturing,” said Steele. The work is funded by the National Research Foundation under its 29th Competitive Research Programme, was published in Applied Materials Today earlier in 2026, and the intellectual property is filed through NTUitive.
The partner
Motherson makes automotive and aerospace components; Dhruv Mehra, Director of Motherson Singapore, is quoted for the company in the announcement.
tiles.src: NTU News, 12 Nov 2026: NTU, Motherson to develop magnetic technology to cut manufacturing time and energy use

tiles.cap: A metre of string across your ears: pluck it and you hear a note nobody else can
tiles.nums: the pitch of a string rises with the square root of its tension, and rises as the string gets shorter; the sound is so quiet that nobody close to you is disturbed
tiles.p1: Take a piece of string at least 1 m long. Put the middle behind your head, bring the two halves forward across your ears so the string crosses each ear opening, and hold the loose ends together in front of your face. Pluck. You hear your string, but so quietly that, the Exploratorium says, you will not disturb other people even if they are close to you. Pull tighter: the note goes up. Slide your hand along to shorten the string while keeping the pull the same: higher again.
tiles.p2: The rule, from the Exploratorium: frequency is proportional to the square root of the tension and inversely proportional to the length; higher frequency is a higher note.
deep: Two knobs

Tension and length are the two things you can change. Double the tension and the frequency rises by √2, about 1.41 times; halve the length at the same tension and it doubles. Try to hear the difference between the two moves.
Why only you
The Exploratorium does not say why the sound stays with you; ask a friend to stand a hand’s width away and report what they hear, then swap places.
The Exploratorium’s joke
“Many city bus services do not allow people to play loud music on buses,” the Exploratorium notes; a head harp keeps you within the rules, and you get “more room as others move away from you.”

tiles.cap: Life’s last common ancestor was alive 4.2 billion years ago, with about 2,600 proteins
tiles.nums: the window between Earth becoming habitable and LUCA, the last universal common ancestor of everything alive today, by the estimates Quanta reports
tiles.p1: For decades the origin-of-life argument was over which came first: RNA, metabolism, or the fatty bubble of a membrane. Quanta’s series this week says the field has moved on, to how messy early chemistry gradually became systems that store information, use energy and evolve. The numbers set the stage: the Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago, the oldest uncontested fossils are about 3.5 billion years old, and LUCA, the last universal common ancestor, is estimated at 4.2 billion years old with roughly 2,600 proteins. Miller’s 1952 spark-in-a-flask experiment made five amino acids.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: at least 6,000 exoplanets are known, around 2,000 of them possibly super-Earths; how easily chemistry becomes biology decides what to expect there.
deep: Three camps

Metabolism-first says life began as self-sustaining cycles of energy-releasing reactions, perhaps at hydrothermal vents; in 2020 Martina Preiner’s team showed vent-like conditions make formate, acetate and pyruvate. Lipid-first says the fatty-acid bubble came first: “You need a container before you can get the chemistry,” says Bruce Damer. RNA-first wants a molecule that both stores information and does chemistry.
Smaller alphabets
Modern proteins use 20 amino acids, but a reduced alphabet of 10 could support early protein folds; one synthetic-cell effort used 36 enzymes. Modern cells run some 1 billion reactions per second.
Crisis is good
“There’s nothing more exciting for a scientific field than a moment of crisis,” says Betül Kaçar. Joanna Masel goes further: “I believe that there were multiple origins of life.”

tiles.cap: The students who got their answers from AI scored 17% worse on the test
tiles.nums: on the exam, after working with a chatbot
tiles.p1: Nearly 1,000 high-school maths students in Turkey were split three ways: problem sets with a plain ChatGPT-style bot, with a version that only gave hints, or with books and notes. While the bot was there the chatbot group looked brilliant, doing 48% better on the problems. Then the AI was taken away for the exam. They scored 17% below the students who never had it.
tiles.p2: Why: if students use these tools as a “crutch” and rely on them, lead author Hamsa Bastani says, they “won’t actually build those fundamental skills.”
deep: The hint-only version was different
Students who used the tutor that refused to give answers did 127% better in the sessions and then matched the book group on the exam. Same technology, different design, different result.
What the researchers concluded

The worry is that students use a plain chatbot as a crutch. The hint-only tutor, designed to guide students instead of directly giving answers, avoided the damage. The researchers call the result a cautionary tale.
Try it on yourself
Next hard problem, ask only for a hint, then close the chat and finish alone. See whether you still remember it a week later.
tiles.src: PNAS, 25 Jun 2025, Bastani et al.: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning (doi 10.1073/pnas.2422633122) · Knowledge at Wharton
